analysis.one_liner: Charges fossil fuel producers a rising per-ton fee and returns most of it as quarterly household rebates.
analysis.headline: The carbon fee bill, introduced by Senator Durbin with no cosponsors, has sat in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote since its introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a fee of $75 per metric ton of carbon dioxide equivalent on oil, coal, and natural gas starting in 2027, rising $10 each year plus inflation, with additional fees on industrial process emissions and fees on imported carbon-intensive goods. Over 75 percent of the money raised would go out as quarterly, tax-free payments to every adult, phasing out for households above $75,000 (single) or $150,000 (joint) in income. The rest would finance a new federal clean-energy finance corporation, payments to farmers who cut emissions, and grants to communities dependent on coal, oil, and gas jobs.
analysis.who_benefits: Adults in lower- and middle-income households, who would receive quarterly payments not counted as income for any federal or state benefits; households below the phaseout thresholds generally gain more from the rebate than they lose in higher fuel prices, since the fee is paid on a per-ton basis by producers and largely passed through in prices. Also benefiting: fossil-fuel-dependent communities receiving transition grants, farmers paid to adopt climate-smart practices, and clean energy and green bank sectors receiving financed projects.

how_it_helps.text: For the first 10 fiscal years, at least 75 percent of fee revenue is apportioned to quarterly carbon fee rebate payments for every adult resident, rising to 80 percent thereafter.

Rebate payments are excluded from gross income for federal tax purposes and are not counted as income or resources in determining eligibility or benefit levels under any federal program or federally financed state or local program.

The bill appropriates $7.5 billion for each of fiscal years 2026 and 2027 to capitalize a new Climate Change Finance Corporation that makes grants and 75 percent loan guarantees for clean energy, grid, transit, and climate-resilience projects, with at least 40 percent of grant funds required to go to prioritized disadvantaged communities.

It appropriates $5 billion for each of fiscal years 2026 and 2027 for transition grants to communities affected by changes in carbon-intensive industries, covering job training, reemployment assistance, early-retirement subsidies, cleanup of coal ash, abandoned mines and orphaned wells, and climate-resilience construction, with prevailing-wage and Buy America requirements attached.
The bill creates an agricultural program paying producers to adopt measurable climate-smart practices, funded at 7 percent of the annual rebate allocation for the first 10 fiscal years.

analysis.who_pays: Producers, refiners, and importers of crude oil, coal, and natural gas owe the fee on every ton of fuel they sell, and the costs are largely passed through to consumers in fuel prices. Higher-income households, whose rebates phase out at 5 percent per $1,000 of income above $75,000 (single) or $150,000 (joint), would bear a net cost, as would energy-intensive businesses facing the fee and the border fee on imports.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and higher-income households

drawbacks.text: The fee starts at $75 per ton and rises $10 per year plus inflation, which would raise fuel prices across the economy; the rebate is a flat per-person payment that does not scale with household energy use, so some high-usage households could be net losers.

The rebate phases out at 5 percent of the payment for every $1,000 of income above $75,000 (single filer) or $150,000 (joint filer), which can create steep effective marginal tax rates for households near the thresholds.

The fee initially applies only to fossil fuels, set against a target equal to 63 percent of 2018 covered-fuel emissions in 2027; fees on industrial process and fugitive emissions do not begin until 2029, so a large share of industrial emissions is untouched in the first years.

The bill appropriates a combined $100 billion for fiscal years 2026 and 2027 before any fee revenue arrives ($37.5 billion for initial rebates, $7.5 billion for the finance corporation, and $5 billion for transition grants in each year), and it creates a new independent federal agency governed by a seven-member presidentially appointed board.

Border fee adjustments on carbon-intensive imports and refunds for exports could create trade friction with countries that do not price carbon, and the bill requires a fee rebate on exported fuels and carbon-intensive products.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is progressive: because the fee is roughly proportional to fuel use while the rebate is flat per adult, most lower- and middle-income households come out ahead on net, and the money flowing to them is untaxed and does not count against public benefits. The costs fall first on fossil fuel producers and, through higher prices, on consumers generally, with the heaviest net burdens on high-income households and high fuel users. The main honest objections are the price shock of a $75 starting fee, the rapid rebate phaseout near income thresholds, the late coverage of industrial process emissions, and the $100 billion in front-loaded appropriations that must be financed before fee revenue fully arrives.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on September 4, 2025; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has had no hearing, no cosponsors, and no vote, while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on September 4, 2025 and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Finance.
The bill has no cosponsors, according to the official cosponsor list.

The bill would impose a carbon fee starting at $75 per metric ton of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2027, rising by $10 annually plus inflation, with faster increases if cumulative emissions exceed statutory targets, and would add a fee on non-fuel industrial emissions beginning in 2029 and carbon border fee adjustments on imports and refunds for exports.

At least 75 percent of fee revenue would be apportioned to quarterly rebate payments for each adult, with the remainder split among a new Climate Change Finance Corporation (15 percent), transition assistance grants (10 percent), and agricultural decarbonization payments (7 percent of the rebate allocation) during the first 10 fiscal years.
No committee action beyond the referral appears in the bill's action history, and the Congress is still in session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No outcome has occurred yet. The status quo favors the entities that would owe the fee: fossil fuel producers, refiners, and importers, along with higher-income households that would have been net payers, benefit from the bill's lack of progress. Low-income households, for whom the bill's rebates would have been net gains, are the party that has lost the opportunity so far.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers, via continued inaction

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; sole sponsor of S. 2712
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over the tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Took no further action on the bill after its referral; no hearing or markup appears in the record.

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill since its referral.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and the bill has one Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Oil, coal, and natural gas producers and refiners
industries.note: Covered entities would owe $75 per metric ton of carbon dioxide equivalent on every unit of fuel sold or used starting in 2027, plus fees on fugitive and process emissions starting in 2029. They can pass costs to consumers in fuel prices, but the rebate design leaves most low- and middle-income households ahead on net, so the industry's financial interest runs against the bill's main public benefit.

industries.industry: Clean energy, green banks, and renewable manufacturers
industries.note: A new Climate Change Finance Corporation with $7.5 billion in initial annual capitalization would finance solar, wind, geothermal, storage, EV and transit deployment with 75 percent loan guarantees and grants, prioritizing disadvantaged communities. The rising carbon fee also makes clean alternatives relatively cheaper every year.

industries.industry: Carbon-intensive manufacturers (steel, aluminum, cement, glass, chemicals, paper)
industries.note: They would owe fees on their industrial process emissions from 2029, but carbon border fees on imported goods and refunds on exported products would shield them from competitors in countries without a carbon price, blunting much of the cost.

industries.industry: Banks, credit unions, and community development lenders
industries.note: Eligible lenders would originate loans backed by 75 percent federal guarantees on clean energy projects, reducing their credit risk while collecting capped guarantee fees, and green bank institutions would receive direct funding.
Farmers would receive payments for verified climate-smart practices, with priority considerations for underserved and low-income producers, funded from the trust fund for 10 fiscal years.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel workers and coal and oil communities
industries.note: Transition grants of $5 billion per year in the initial appropriation would fund retraining, wage-replacement for early retirees, mine reclamation, well plugging, and coal ash cleanup in communities dependent on carbon-intensive industries.

analysis.trajectory: A carbon fee bill with zero cosponsors and no committee action is very unlikely to advance in a Senate Finance Committee that has not scheduled it. Absent a substantial build-up of cosponsors or a change in committee leadership priorities, the bill will probably expire at the end of the 119th Congress without a hearing or vote, as standalone carbon-pricing bills historically have.
